1233.title: Meeting the teacher
1233.hook: a private meeting where the student shows their understanding
1233.howItsDone: In Zen communities, students meet the teacher privately during retreats and regular sittings; in Rinzai practice the meeting often centers on the student's koan, while in Soto practice it is often a conversation about the student's sitting and life.

segments.voice: Yesterday: sesshin, days of silent practice, the mind collected like water drawn into one bowl. Your line: gathering the mind.

In the middle of a silent sesshin, one sound cuts through the hall: a small hand bell. A student rises from the cushion and waits in line outside a closed door. When it's her turn, she goes in, bows, and sits down across from the teacher. Just the two of them; nobody else will hear what's said. She may have a few minutes. She has to show what she understands, not explain it, not quote a book. Show it. Today's word is the name for that meeting: dokusan.
screen: `A HAND BELL IN THE SILENCE.` → `A LINE OUTSIDE A CLOSED DOOR.` → `JUST THE TWO OF THEM.`

segments.voice: First, the word. Dokusan is Japanese, often rendered as going alone to the teacher. Not as a class or a group. Whatever you've been sitting with, you carry into that room yourself. Second, what happens inside differs by school. In Rinzai halls the meeting often turns on a koan. The student presents a response, and the teacher may accept it, ask a question, or ring the bell to end the meeting, which means: go back and sit with it more. In Soto communities, dokusan is often a quieter conversation about practice: how the sitting is going, where the mind keeps getting stuck. Different shape, same doorway. Third, seen, not read. Zen tradition describes itself as a teaching passed from one person to another, not only through books. A teacher can't see your understanding in your notes. They see it in how you walk in, how you answer, whether you hesitate or hide behind a clever line. Fourth, your understanding, right now. A lot of everyday talk about what people think happens at a safe distance: in text, in summary, after the fact. Dokusan asks for something rarer: your actual understanding, now, in front of someone who's paying attention. Even being turned away is part of it. The bell rings, the student bows, and walks back to the cushion with the question still alive.
screen: `GOING ALONE TO THE TEACHER.` · `A KOAN, OR A TALK ABOUT PRACTICE.` · `SEEN, NOT READ.` · `YOUR UNDERSTANDING, RIGHT NOW.` · then, large: `FACE TO FACE.`

segments.voice: Imagine a quiet room and someone across from you who simply asks: how is your practice, really? Find one honest sentence, not the polished answer: maybe I keep starting and stopping, maybe I don't know what I'm doing, maybe one small thing that's going well. Then let it rest, and come back to the breath.
Dokusan. A private meeting between a Zen student and teacher, where the student shows their understanding, and the teacher meets it directly. Today's word.
Your line: face to face. In that room, understanding isn't explained or quoted; it's shown. Until tomorrow.

1234.title: Walking between sittings
1234.hook: slow walking meditation between periods of zazen
1234.howItsDone: In Zen halls, kinhin follows each period of zazen: practitioners walk in a line around the room with hands held at the chest, slowly in many Soto communities and more briskly in some Rinzai ones, until a bell calls them back to sit.

segments.voice: Yesterday: dokusan, going alone to the teacher to show what you understand. Your line: face to face.

The bell rings, and a period of zazen ends. Nobody heads for the door. Everyone stands, turns, and walks in a slow line around the hall. One foot. Then, much later it seems, the other. Hands held together in front of the chest, eyes lowered. Someone glancing through the window might think the whole room has slowed to half speed. In a way, it has. Knees that ached get to stretch, and the sitting goes on, upright and moving. Today's word: kinhin.
screen: `THE BELL ENDS THE SITTING.` → `NOBODY LEAVES.` → `A SLOW LINE AROUND THE HALL.`

segments.voice: First, sitting carried into motion. Kinhin comes between periods of zazen. The body gets a rest from crossed legs, but the attention doesn't take a break. Second, the form. The hands are held in a particular way, often one hand closed loosely and the other wrapped over it, resting at the chest. In many Soto halls, each breath carries the walker forward about half the length of a foot: step on the out-breath, pause, step again. Slow enough that walking stops being travel and becomes something you can feel: heel, sole, toes, weight shifting. Third, the schools differ. In some Rinzai halls kinhin is brisk, almost a quick march, and it can wake a sleepy body in a hurry. Soto halls often keep it very slow. Neither is a mistake. Both are the hall moving together, in one line, at one pace, nobody passing anybody. Fourth, attention learns to stand up. The walk from the cushion to the door is the first step of the walk home. Kinhin is the hinge. The point isn't to move strangely forever. It's to discover that attention can stand up with you, step out the door, and come along to the bus stop. And when the bell ends kinhin, everyone goes straight back to the cushion, the same attention sitting down again.
screen: `SITTING, CARRIED INTO MOTION.` · `HANDS AT THE CHEST, HALF A STEP.` · `SLOW IN ONE HALL, BRISK IN ANOTHER.` · `ATTENTION LEARNS TO STAND UP.` · then, large: `WALKING ZEN.`

segments.voice: If you have room, stand and rest your hands loosely together at your chest; breathe out and move one foot forward about half its length, feel the weight arrive, then breathe in and pause. If standing isn't easy, do it seated: lift and place one foot, then the other, with the breath.
Kinhin. Walking meditation between periods of zazen: slow in many halls, brisk in some, always the same attention, carried on foot. Today's word.
Your line: walking zen. The same attention as sitting, carried on foot. Same time tomorrow.

1235.title: Bowls
1235.hook: the formal meal eaten from nested bowls, nothing wasted
1235.howItsDone: In many Zen monasteries and retreats, meals are eaten in the meditation hall in the oryoki style: participants unwrap a set of nested bowls, chant meal verses, receive food in silence, signal when they have enough, and clean their bowls with hot water at the end.

segments.voice: Yesterday: kinhin, the slow walk between sittings, attention carried on foot. Your line: walking zen.

A small bundle sits in front of each person in the hall: a cloth, tied with a neat knot. At the sound of a clapper, everyone unties it at the same moment. Inside are bowls, one fitted inside the next like a set of measuring cups, plus a cloth, a spoon, chopsticks and a little spatula. The bowls come out in order and are set in a row. Servers walk the line with pots of food. Nobody talks. Nobody reaches across. At the end, the bowls go back exactly as they came out, clean. Today's word: oryoki.
screen: `A BUNDLE TIED IN A CLOTH.` → `BOWLS NESTED ONE INSIDE ANOTHER.` → `NOTHING WASTED.`

segments.voice: First, the word. Oryoki is Japanese, often rendered as just enough: a vessel that holds exactly what is needed. You don't heap, and you don't leave a pile. Second, one hand raised. When the server stops in front of you with a pot, you hold up a hand to signal enough. You take what you'll actually eat. It's a tiny decision, made in silence with every serving, and it's the heart of the form: noticing, before the food lands, how much you really need. Third, the end of the meal. Hot water is poured into the bowls. Each person cleans their bowl with the little spatula, moves the water to the next bowl and cleans that one too, then drinks the rinse water. Tradition says a little of the water is set aside and offered to beings who go hungry. Not a grain of rice is left to throw away. Fourth, no meal on autopilot. Before eating, the hall chants verses on how much work brought the food here, and on eating to sustain practice, not to indulge. Oryoki takes something as automatic as eating and makes it impossible to do on autopilot. On an ordinary workday, with a sandwich at a desk, the question it leaves is simple: how much is enough, and did I notice?
screen: `A VESSEL THAT HOLDS JUST ENOUGH.` · `ONE HAND RAISED: ENOUGH.` · `THE BOWLS RINSED, THE WATER DRUNK.` · `NO MEAL ON AUTOPILOT.` · then, large: `JUST ENOUGH.`

segments.voice: Picture the next thing you'll eat, a meal or a snack, in front of you, and before it arrives, ask the oryoki question: how much is actually enough? Not what's polite, not what's on the plate. Notice the answer and whether it surprises you, then picture the last bite and the empty bowl, clean, with nothing to throw away.
Oryoki. The formal Zen meal eaten from nested bowls: take just what you need, eat it with care, and leave nothing to waste. Today's word.
Your line: just enough. Not a grain left to throw away. Rest well.

1236.title: Work practice
1236.hook: cleaning, gardening and cooking as meditation
1236.howItsDone: In Zen monasteries and at many retreats, a daily work period called samu has everyone, teachers included, clean, garden and cook in silence, treating the work as meditation rather than a break from it.

segments.voice: Yesterday: oryoki, the nested bowls, and taking just what you need. Your line: just enough.

The tools have gone missing. That's how a story about the Chan teacher Baizhang begins, as tradition tells it. He's old, and his students worry about him working in the fields, so they hide his hoe and his rake. Baizhang doesn't argue. He just doesn't eat that day. When they ask why, the answer that has come down is short: a day without work is a day without food. The tools come back. In Zen monasteries today, a whole period is set aside for what Baizhang refused to give up. Today's word: samu.
screen: `THE TOOLS GO MISSING.` → `THE OLD TEACHER WON'T EAT.` → `NO WORK, NO FOOD.`

segments.voice: First, what samu is. It's the work period in a Zen monastery or retreat: sweeping, raking, scrubbing floors, weeding, chopping vegetables, cleaning toilets. It's done in silence, usually for a set stretch of the day, and everyone takes part, teachers included. Second, the broom is the cushion now. Chores aren't a break from meditation; meditation doesn't stop when you pick up a broom. The attention that watched the breath now watches the bristles on the floor, the water in the bucket, the weed coming up with its roots. Third, no nice jobs, no rushing. Nobody is meant to rush to finish, and nobody picks the nice job. You're handed a task and do it fully, whether it's polishing a statue or unclogging a drain. Some teachers say the toilets are a good place to see your own mind: what you resist is right there in the bucket. Fourth, the dishes might be the practice. Baizhang's line ties the meal to the work, and the work to the way. Feeding the community and keeping it clean is the practice, not a distraction from it. So a sink full of dishes isn't standing between you and practice. It might be the practice, if you let it.
screen: `SWEEPING, WEEDING, SCRUBBING.` · `THE BROOM IS THE CUSHION NOW.` · `NO NICE JOBS, NO RUSHING.` · `THE DISHES MIGHT BE THE PRACTICE.` · then, large: `WORK IS ZEN.`

segments.voice: Clean one small thing within reach, slowly and with full attention: a phone screen, a cup, a corner of the table, your glasses. Feel the cloth against the surface, notice the moment your mind wants to hurry or drift to the next thing, and come back to this one surface. When it's clean, set it down and sit with the breath.
Samu. Work practice in Zen: cleaning, gardening, cooking, done in silence and with full attention, as meditation in motion. Today's word.
Your line: work is zen. No work, no food, and no chore outside the way. See you tomorrow, broom and all.

1237.title: The wooden board
1237.hook: a wooden board struck to call the monks, often inscribed: life and death are grave, time passes swiftly
1237.howItsDone: In Zen monasteries and centers a wooden board called the han hangs outside the meditation hall and is struck in a set rhythm to call people to sit; it often carries an inscription about the urgency of life and death and the swift passing of time.

segments.voice: Yesterday: samu, work as practice, where a sink of dishes can be the way. Your line: work is zen.

Clack. A pause. Clack. Clack. Then faster and faster, a wooden rattle rolling across the courtyard until it runs out, and stops. Outside a Zen hall there often hangs a thick, heavy board of wood, and someone stands before it with a mallet. The sound tells everyone: come to sit. Walk up close and you may see words brushed on its face. Their message, in plain English: life and death are a great matter. Time passes swiftly.
screen: `CLACK. A PAUSE. CLACK.` → `A BOARD OUTSIDE THE HALL.` → `WORDS ON ITS FACE.`

segments.voice: First, what it is. In Japanese it's called the han: a plank of hard wood hung by cords, struck with a wooden mallet. It calls the community to zazen, and in some places marks the start of the day's sittings. Its sound isn't musical like a bell. It's dry and blunt, more a knock on the door than a song. Second, the words. The inscription varies, but the common message, in paraphrase, runs like this: the matter of life and death is great; everything passes, and passes quickly; wake up; don't waste this time. It's not decoration. It's the reason for the sitting, written on the thing that calls you to sit. Third, the board wears through. Struck day after day, the wood slowly wears down, and some boards end up with a hollow, or a hole right through the center where the mallet lands. The board teaches impermanence by being used up. Every strike that calls the monks takes a little of the board away. Fourth, not hurry, notice. Time passes swiftly is not a threat. It's a reminder, said plainly, the way a friend might tap your shoulder. In Zen, remembering that life is short isn't meant to make people anxious. It's meant to wake them up to this hour, this breath, this conversation, while it's here. The board doesn't say hurry. It says notice, because this won't come again.
screen: `A PLANK OF WOOD, A MALLET.` · `WORDS: LIFE AND DEATH ARE GREAT.` · `THE BOARD WEARS THROUGH.` · `NOT HURRY. NOTICE.` · then, large: `TIME PASSES SWIFTLY.`

segments.voice: Tap something gently, a table, a book, your own knee, and listen until the sound is completely gone. Tap again, letting each one be a small han, a call back to this moment, and notice that the last sound has already passed. After a few, stop tapping and simply sit, listening.
The wooden board. The han, struck to call a Zen community to sit, and often inscribed with a reminder: life and death are a great matter, time passes swiftly. Today's word.
Your line: time passes swiftly. The board is calling, gently, and this hour is here. Twelve thirty-seven days on the path.

1238.title: Chanting in Zen
1238.hook: the Heart Sutra, the four vows, the names of the ancestors
1238.howItsDone: Zen communities hold chanting services, often morning and evening, where the Heart Sutra, the four bodhisattva vows, dedications and sometimes the names of the lineage ancestors are chanted together in a steady tone, often kept in time by a wooden drum.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the han, the wooden board that calls the hall to sit, and reminds it that life is short. Your line: time passes swiftly.

Zen has a reputation for silence, so the morning service can come as a surprise. Before breakfast, the whole hall stands or kneels and chants, loudly, in one low, steady pitch. A hollow wooden drum, carved in the shape of a fish, keeps the beat: tok, tok, tok. Nobody is performing. Nobody is singing harmony. Voices that don't match blend into one sound that seems to fill the floorboards. Then it stops, and the silence afterward feels different.
screen: `A SILENT SCHOOL THAT CHANTS.` → `ONE LOW PITCH, ONE BEAT.` → `THE SILENCE AFTER.`

segments.voice: First, the Heart Sutra. You met it earlier on this path: the short text where Avalokiteshvara sees that all five heaps are empty, and tells Shariputra that form is emptiness and emptiness is form. Zen halls chant it often, in Japanese, Chinese, Korean, Vietnamese or English, depending on the community. Chanting it isn't studying it. The aim is to let the text pass through the body until it's breath, not argument. Second, the four vows: the bodhisattva vows, said together, often at the end of a service. In plain paraphrase: beings are without number, I vow to free them. Delusions never run out, I vow to end them. The gates of the teaching are without limit, I vow to enter them. The Buddha's way is beyond reach, I vow to embody it. Each vow names something impossible, and promises it anyway. Third, the ancestors. Some services chant the lineage: the Buddha, then teacher after teacher, down to the founders of that community's line. A family tree said aloud, a reminder that this practice came hand to hand, through people. Fourth, one voice, one body. Chanting uses breath, belly and throat. It's hard to chant at full voice and think about lunch. And chanting together makes the hall one body, the way kinhin made it one line. Zen silence and Zen chanting aren't opposites. Both are ways of being entirely here.
screen: `THE HEART SUTRA, AS BREATH.` · `FOUR VOWS, EACH IMPOSSIBLE.` · `THE ANCESTORS, NAME BY NAME.` · `ONE VOICE, ONE BODY.` · then, large: `CHANTING ZEN.`

segments.voice: Sit up and take a full breath into the belly. If you practice, say the four vows in your community's wording; if not, say today's plain paraphrase slowly, in one low, steady tone, from beings are without number through all four, without worrying about perfect words. Then sit in the quiet that follows.
Chanting in Zen. The Heart Sutra, the four vows and the names of the ancestors, chanted together in one low voice, as practice for the whole body. Today's word.
Your line: chanting zen. Voices that don't match, blended into one low sound. See you tomorrow.

1239.title: The cook's instructions
1239.hook: Dogen's instructions for the cook: treat rice and water as your own eyes
1239.howItsDone: In Soto Zen monasteries the head cook (tenzo) is a senior role, and Dogen's Instructions for the Cook (Tenzo Kyokun) is still read as a guide to treating kitchen work, and daily work in general, as practice.

segments.voice: This week walked through a Zen hall: the teacher's room, the slow walk, the bowls, the broom, the board, the chant. Yesterday's line: chanting zen. Now the week closes in the kitchen.

Midday, blazing sun, stone pavement too hot to stand on. An old monk with no hat, a bamboo staff in his hand, is spreading mushrooms out to dry, sweat pouring off him. A young visitor from Japan, Dogen, asks him: why are you doing this yourself? Why not let a helper do it? The old cook answers, in paraphrase: others are not me. Dogen tries again: then why now, in this heat? The answer: if not now, when? Dogen tells this story in a short text he wrote for monastery cooks.
screen: `AN OLD COOK IN THE NOON SUN.` → `OTHERS ARE NOT ME.` → `IF NOT NOW, WHEN?`

segments.voice: First, the kitchen is a meditation hall. In a Zen monastery the head cook, the tenzo, is a senior post, given to someone whose practice is trusted. Dogen's instructions treat the kitchen as a meditation hall: planning meals, washing rice, tending the fire, none of it beneath anyone, none of it separate from the way. Second, the eyes. Dogen tells the cook, in paraphrase, to look after the rice and water as carefully as your own eyes: gently, never carelessly, never roughly. He also says to look for sand while washing the rice, and for rice while throwing out the sand, so not one grain is lost and not one stone gets through. Third, no plain dish, no fancy dish. A simple broth made with care, he says in paraphrase, is no lower than a rich dish, and a rich dish is no higher. Every pot gets the same eyes. Fourth, not someone else, not later. The old cook turned down the easy way out twice. Dogen writes that he had nothing more to say, and walked away seeing how much the cook's work matters. The way was in this too: the mushrooms, the heat, done by your own hands, now. For anyone who has stood at a stove at the end of a long day, that's a striking thought: the pot of pasta is not in the way of a deeper life.
screen: `THE KITCHEN IS A MEDITATION HALL.` · `RICE AND WATER, LIKE YOUR EYES.` · `NO PLAIN DISH, NO FANCY DISH.` · `NOT SOMEONE ELSE. NOT LATER.` · then, large: `AS YOUR OWN EYES.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind the next thing you'll prepare, even toast or a cup of tea, and picture your hands doing it: the water running, the bread, the knife. Now picture doing it the tenzo's way, as carefully as you'd handle your own eyes, with no hurry and nothing beneath you. Notice what changes, then let it go and rest in the breath.
The cook's instructions. Dogen's teaching for the monastery cook: treat the rice and water as your own eyes, and cook every meal as practice. Today's word.
Your line: as your own eyes. Every pot, plain or fancy, gets the same care. That's the week.

chat.says: Why did the old cook dry mushrooms himself in the heat, instead of letting a helper?
options: Others are not me, and if not now, when? For him, the kitchen work was the way itself.
He didn't trust the helpers to do it properly, so he did all of it alone.
It was a penance he had to finish before he was allowed to meditate.
chat.meaning: The old cook told Dogen: others are not me; if not now, when? Dogen's instructions treat the kitchen as practice.
